overview: The Khiva Khanate grew from Uzbek Arabshahid rule in Khorezm, established in 1511. Its oasis towns and irrigated fields lay around the lower Amu Darya. The map shows 1530 to 1783, not the state’s full lifetime. Its broad, nearly unchanged outline should not be read as proof of constant control across deserts and steppe. Later buildings and documents below are dated separately.

periods.title: Earlier centers
periods.summary: The Arabshahid state initially had centers at Vazir and Urgench.

periods.title: Khiva becomes the capital
periods.summary: Under Arab Muhammad I, Khiva became the capital; subsequent rulers expanded irrigation and historical writing.

periods.title: Invasion and rival powers
periods.summary: Nader Shah’s occupation was followed by political struggles and growing Qonghrat influence.

items.text: In the seventeenth century, Abul Ghazi and other rulers developed canals and distributed newly irrigated land among Uzbek groups. Waterworks helped turn political promises into farms. Crown land could be leased or cultivated by enslaved workers, so expansion also depended on deeply unequal control of land and labor.

Keeping water moving required regular digging. In Khiva, government-organized compulsory work was called bigar; its crucial canal-building and repair duty was qazu. Workers maintained major channels and dams that supported agriculture. This was an obligation imposed on people, not a cheerful volunteer gardening club.

Smaller channels had a different organization. Local communities arranged work on sub-canals, which was not counted as the government’s bigar. A farm could therefore depend on both neighborhood cooperation and state demands. The distinction helps explain why irrigation involved social organization as well as engineering.

Captivity was part of the khanate’s economy. Enslaved people included Persians captured in raids and Russians seized on frontier routes; they worked in households and fields. Nader freed captives in 1740, but slavery returned and survived until its abolition after the Russian conquest of 1873.

Surviving traditional Khivan houses enclose a courtyard, with reception space under a portico supported by carved wooden posts and more private rooms beyond. UNESCO identifies eighteenth- and twentieth-century variants. These homes show how builders arranged privacy, hospitality and outdoor space within a closely packed town.

A clever feature of traditional Khivan homes is the tall ulu-aivan, an open porch facing a lower porch across the courtyard. Builders aligned it to catch the wind and guide air inward. Architecture supplied some of the cooling: an impressive trick before anyone could reach for an electric fan.

Djuma Mosque was rebuilt in 1788 to 1789, just after this map record ends. Its roofed prayer hall incorporated elements from older buildings. Reuse preserved earlier craftsmanship inside a later structure: the age of a carved support need not be the age of the building surrounding it.

A later school shows how education fitted into a working city. Alla-Kuli’s madrasa, built in 1835, occupied a difficult site beside the eastern gate and above the market entrance. Its builders had to accommodate existing streets and structures. Monumental learning institutions were neighbors of everyday commerce.

sections.title: Historians, handwriting and an original title

items.text: Abul Ghazi was both ruler and historian. During ten years in Isfahan after 1629, he studied Persian and Arabic histories alongside traditions remembered from home. His later historical works were written in Chaghatay Turkic. Knowledge moved across languages, courts and personal journeys, not only through conquest.

شجرۂ تراكمه, Shajara-yi Tarakima, means “Genealogy of the Turkmen.” Abul Ghazi wrote this Chaghatay Turkic work in 1659 to 1660. The sample uses the title’s modern scholarly Arabic-script typography; it is not a facsimile of his handwriting. Its family histories drew on earlier books and traditions.

Another history, the Shajara-yi Turk, outlived its first author. Anusha Khan commissioned the scholar Mulla Mahmudi to continue his father’s work. Mahmudi had also taught Anusha. Research on manuscript 851 in Tashkent suggests it may preserve the continuator’s own hand, although that remains a scholarly argument.

That manuscript contains inserted leaves and writing squeezed into margins. Toshov identifies an added account of China on folios 84 to 86, with nearby text moved into a margin. Handwritten history could be revised and expanded. Before “insert paragraph,” a writer sometimes had to insert actual paper.

Writing also handled practical government business. Around eleven thousand texts seized by Russian forces in 1873 form the collection called the Archive of the Khans of Khiva. Records in Chaghatay concern taxes, property, military affairs and diplomacy: the paperwork behind royal power survives alongside literary books.

sections.title: A later adventure in melon growing

items.text: In 1875, long after the map’s endpoint, Hungarian grower Bertalan Ónody visited Khiva to investigate farming. Muhammad Rahim II permitted his travels and supplied a guide familiar with local agriculture. The visitor needed local expertise: arriving with an enthusiasm for melons was only the beginning of learning how they grew.

Ónody took seeds home and published accounts of Khivan crops and melon cultivation in 1877. His attempt to turn the imported seeds into a profitable business failed. The episode captures both the appeal of the region’s produce and the difficulty of moving an agricultural success from one setting to another.

ending.text: The map’s 1783 endpoint was not a collapse. A reduced khanate survived Russia’s invasion of 1873 as a protectorate. Bolshevik conquest ended the last khan’s rule in February 1920. The monarchy disappeared, while Khorezm’s communities and cultural traditions continued.
